speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Parkdale asked me a question relating to the increase in hepatitis cases over the past year.
The question of viral hepatitis has been of some concern to my department and provincial and local departments of health, and to the medical profession. Some time ago I established an expert committee on viral hepatitis as a subcommittee of the dominion council of health. This committee reported to the session of the dominion council of health sitting in Ottawa at the present time.
In its current report-and I would emphasize that the committee will be continuing to work on this problem-recommendations were made for the prevention of this disease. They included proposals with regard to sanitary control and the use of gamma globulin primarily as a preventive measure. The deputy ministers of health of the provinces are members of council, and in this way the information has been made available to the provincial departments of health. I recognize that viral hepatitis is an important public health problem, not only in Canada but in many other countries, and we will continue to take active steps to keep this disease under control.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ABSENCE OF ESKIMO DELEGATES FROM SUDBURY MEETING
speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for the Northwest Territories inquired whether the absence

of Eskimo representatives from the Indian-Eskimo association meetings in Sudbury was due to the refusal of the government to assist in transportation.
In reply I should like to point out that the Indian-Eskimo Association of Canada is a private and voluntary organization incorporated on December 21, 1959, in response to the growing interest in northern Canada resulting from the government's program of northern development. My department has taken a close and continuing interest in the excellent work of the association. The federal government, through the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, provides financial assistance by way of grants to support the activities of the association. I am advised that, a portion of this year's grant helped to defray the cost of the meetings held in Sudbury.
I must, however, confess that I am somewhat puzzled by the question, since no request for assistance with respect to transportation was received by my department. Therefore there can, of course, be no question of refusal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: At the previous sitting of this committee we were considering paragraph 3 of the resolution. Shall the paragraph carry?

Mr. Chairman, on November 2 when I was discussing paragraph 3 of the resolution I had pointed out the tremendous loss to Canada in the ten year period 1950-60 of educated persons by emigration to the United States. I was quoting from the Labour Gazette of January 31, 1962, and I should like to put some figures on the record to indicate what I believe members on all sides of the house will agree constitutes a most serious drain upon the resources of Canada. I quote:
Of the types of professionals who emigrated to the United States during the 1950-60 period nurses were the most conspicuous: they made up 30.5 per cent of the total of professional emigrants.
Some hon. members may say that the loss to Canada of nurses is not serious. I do know that the medical profession in my province is saying that, unfortunately, a high percentage of these nurses who are going to the United States are specialized nurses, specialists in such things as x-ray treatment and so on.
Engineers constituted 18.7 per cent. Other groups were accountants and auditors (5.4 per cent), draftsmen (5.2 per cent), . . . scientists (4.4 per cent), physicians and surgeons (4.8 per cent), and technicians (7.4 per cent).
I put those figures on the record, Mr. Chairman, because I believe that the effect of this five year undertaking to allow to these corporations 150 per cent of the cost of research done in Canada in relation to what they expended in the year previous is a good thing and will be supported by this side of the house. However, I do suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that this is going to be of benefit to a relatively small number of companies in Canada. I turn to the proceedings of the special committee on research in 1960, and the evidence of the late Dr. Steacie of the national research council. At page 14 he is reported as saying:
The extreme case would probably be that of applied chemistry as compared to building research- the chemical industry in Canada consists essentially of a dozen quite large firms, whereas the building industry consists of thousands of contractors.
In the chemical industry you will always have plenty of people to contact, but in the construction business you have no one to contact concerning research problems, and you will have to find out what is bothering them, and then use your own initiative.
I suggest that the effect of this preference granted to firms will probably be to return to Canada some research that is done by gigantic United States firms for their Canadian subsidiaries, and that is a good thing. However, I ask myself what provision is being made for research in Canada, and I have to return to the national research council. I find that, according to the revised estimates, there is actually a reduction imposed upon the national research council. While there are increases granted in respect of salaries there is a reduction of $2,581,243 brought about by an obvious withdrawal in construction and acquisition of buildings, works, lands and equipment, and in its place there is an increase of $1 million providing assistance toward research in industry.
Here we have a situation in which the government is declaring itself in favour of research in Canada, but it provides an increase of only $1 million, and the small firms in Canada that are so preoccupied with their daily business that they cannot do their own research-they have neither the facilities, the ability nor the time-must look to the national research council to do the research for them.
The national research council is doing a splendid job. It is doing much of its work through our universities, either in pure research or business research, but we must compare this item of $1 million with the

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Are not the figures he is using in respect to the United States and the United Kingdom the amount which is spent for research in the totality? And if a comparison is to be made should it not take into account not only the $1 million but the total estimates for national research and the funds which the provinces provide in Canada, of which there are no counterparts in existence in the United Kingdom?
I have searched through all the material I could obtain, and I have some figures which indicate total research expenditures in Canada at $150 million for all sources and at all levels.

speechtext: Is that public moneys?

Public and private, but I rather think mostly private. I hope that this special item of $1 million is merely a token, and that the government and front benches regard it as a token.
We in Canada can do certain things extremely well, and we are doing some research extremely well. There is a private company in the city of Vancouver which I have no desire to advertise, Sandwell and Associates, which is now an international concern. It has on its staff men of international reputation from all parts of the world, and it is doing work in all parts of the world.
More and more of the machinery used in our pulp and paper industry and sawmills is being manufactured in Canada. It will be of interest to some hon. members who come from areas of lumber production to learn that one small sawmill in my riding employs 12 men on two shifts, in other words 24 men per day, and that mill is turning out 200,000 board feet of timber a day with machinery manufactured in the city of New Westminster and designed in the province of British Columbia. The Sandwell company is doing work all over the world and specializes in the production of machinery plants for pulp and paper mills. It has some excellent technicians, but that company will not benefit as a result of this action by the government.
We in Canada also have great experience in hard rock mining and could do more research in that field. There are many other areas where research is required, but I shall wind up by saying that of all the nations in the world, Canada today requires a greater national and unifying purpose. I think that

has been demonstrated in this house in recent weeks. I shall not suggest that the expenditure of great sums of money on technology, science and research is the way to get that unifying influence, but I believe it could be one of the ways to help in getting it.
The age in which we live is a new age of discovery, and before the next generation matures I believe we shall have conquered many of the maladies of mankind. We shall have conquered heart disease, cancer and a great many other diseases. Also we in Canada can make a very great contribution toward the furthering of science in the emerging countries of the world, but we are losing a tremendous opportunity by not doing it now. With our great variety of industries we have an opportunity to bring young scientists from the emerging countries in greater numbers than we have hitherto, and teach them our skills and our technology.
I hope the minister will be able to tell us that supplementary estimates will be introduced for research. I suspect they will be, and I trust this very small amount will be increased to extend the advantages of research through the national research council to small companies in Canada. Those companies will not benefit much by the legislation the minister has introduced at the moment. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I have just been handed a copy of the resolutions on ways and means now under consideration, and I am particularly interested in the one dealing with the Income Tax Act. Mention is made in paragraph 3 of tax deductions allowed to those who go in for scientific research.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that regardless of the particulars mentioned in that paragraph, one thing must be borne in mind. At the present time, the more you promote and assist industrial research and automation, the more you improve the products and develop new needs. Those new needs will result in an increased production and, consequently, we will have to build more factories.
I should like to point out that our group endorses any tax deduction which tends to promote research and development of production methods in our country.
But I should like to make a suggestion to the Minister of National Revenue. Apart from those deductions for research expenditures, the minister should advise his inspectors that, when they audit the books of companies, they

must, not only allow them the deductions they are entitled to, but also leave our industrialists in peace and give them a change to breathe freely.
Nowadays, even if industrialists are given all sorts of privileges, the inspectors come around and cancel everything, which brings about increased expenditures, since accounting operations, red tape and what not are multiplied.
We approve this income tax deduction, but our suggestion to the minister would be to warn his inspectors to stop making trouble and causing increased costs for businessmen and manufacturers in our country.
Let us submit to robbery.

Mr. Chairman, we are in favour of the tax deductions which are being granted today, but, nevertheless, I would ask the Prime Minister to do away with all that useless red tape in the collection of that money. No other department, in my opinion, causes more trouble to Canadians.
The minister should be concerned not only with the granting of exemptions, but he should see to it that the inspectors of his department stop making trouble for businessmen. The minister should realize that after having added up all deductions, if an inspector feels that some industrialist, businessman or merchant has not paid the required tax, while the taxpayer is convinced he has submitted a proper return, then a wrong is being inflicted upon that taxpayer, because it is up to him to prove that his return is accurate and to initiate legal proceedings to do so, something which is often very costly.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to refer very briefly to the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver South a few minutes ago. While there is quite a lot in his remarks with which many of us in this committee would agree, it should nevertheless be pointed out that the research facilities of the government are far from being concentrated in just the national research council, as the hon. member seemed to indicate. I have been reading very recently some articles dealing with research, and I came across a series of articles written for industrial Canada which have been reprinted by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. It is there set out that not less than 61 per cent of all research carried out in Canada is financed directly by the federal government, and that the role of government in research has been of immeasurable help in building and expanding Canada's wealth of raw material resources and thus providing a firm base for our manufacturing industry.
It mentions a few of the branches, and I think it is worth while stating those that are concerned with research. We have, for instance, the departments of Agriculture, Fisheries, Northern Affairs and National Resources, Forestry and Trade and Commerce, and more recent entrants have been national defence, national health and welfare, the national research council, of course, and Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd.
Another factor that must be remembered, as was stated by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, is that we are living under a federal system and the provincial governments also have extensive research facilities. I think my own Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is most closely associated with research. I might say that the principal role and purpose of the department is to promote research. I would like to point out that this research is associated very closely indeed with the mining industry, and many of the projects which are entered into by my department are carried out at the specific request of the industry. Moreover, in many cases mining companies may come and use the elaborate laboratory facilities existing in the mines branch on Booth street here in Ottawa, and may carry out experiments there.

All of this has helped to make our mining industry in particular one of the most competitive industries anywhere in the world.
While the government and hon. members here are indeed very much concerned with research, with the role of Canada in research, and the picture of the role of our country and its rank in the changing technological world in which we live, we must nevertheless not belittle the really substantial efforts that are being made by this government, which have been vastly enhanced and increased in the last few years.
Paragraphs 3 and 4 agreed to.
On paragraph 5-

Mr. Chairman, I am puzzled by paragraph 5. One thing I would like to know is just why the computations have to be complicated by speaking of two thirds of 10 per cent, instead of 7.5 per cent, which I would think is the logical way to express it. Another question that comes to my mind is raised by the final phrase in this paragraph, which proposes to repeal the right in computing income to deduct amounts paid to a province as tax on income from logging operations. Does that imply that the government has made some amendments to the federal-provincial agreements under which the provinces continue to levy a tax on logging operation? If so, what has been the nature of those amendments? That is one thing I would like to know.
It seems to me very strange that this government which, in spite of the optimism of the Minister of Finance, has been in grave financial difficulties-he admits that the government has been in very grave financial difficulties-would take steps that would appear to be reducing their income still further in favour of a section of our economy that has been doing very well lately, in fact extraordinarily well. One of the great advantages of the logging industry, at least on the Pacific coast, is that it is given to jurisdictions in revealing the amounts by which it is benefiting from its operations. Earlier this session I pointed out that at the end of the first six months of 1962 one large lumber corporation in British Columbia announced that its profits had increased by 43 per cent over the corresponding period in 1961, and another announced that its profits had increased by 50 per cent over the corresponding period in 1961.
It seems inappropriate to be choosing this section of the economy for generosity on the part of the government. I know, of course, the argument will be made that this is intended to encourage logging corporations to
Income Tax Act
engage in modern silvicultural practices, conservation, reforestation and so on. It is the sort of argument I remember being produced at the time the first of the forest management licences were introduced by legislation in British Columbia. We were told then that we were going to place our forest industry on a rational basis, on a sustained yield basis, that the corporations would undertake to make sure that the forest wealth of British Columbia was maintained and that only the increment would be drawn from. Well, of course, there is no British Columbian who is not aware that the other side of the bargain was never kept.
I am always amused, when I drive through parts of my own constituency, to see large signs informing travellers that they are now entering such and such a tree farm, the implication being that this particular growth of young timber had been brought about by the activities of the lumber corporation concerned. This may fool some people, but it does not fool anyone like myself who has seen that particular piece of land in all its various stages, having passed through it 20 or 25 years before when it was a complete desert-and it was left as a desert until gradually, year by year, natural reforestation began to take effect, without any effort or expenditure being made by the corporation which benefited from the original cutting.
On Vancouver island particularly we also have a serious problem created by the fact that so large a part of our timber holdings is now owned by corporations whose head offices are in New York. It always exasperates me as a Canadian and as a British Columbian to read in the papers of the manner in which such organizations as rod and gun clubs have to go cap in hand, not to a local company but to New York, to find out whether the United States owners of our forests will permit members of their organization to enjoy the recreational possibilities of the Vancouver island forests. On the other hand these forests serve as a recreational centre for a great many of the officials and staffs of those companies who notoriously come up year after year from the United States to hunt and fish, not always within the limits imposed by our game laws, on these private reserves which have been established by the corporations.
I submit that the people of Canada should not be asked, at a time when they are being told by this government to tighten their belts, to further subsidize corporations whose activities are causing growing concern in the province of British Columbia, and whose financial position is revealed again and again

Income Tax Act
in company reports and in statements by company executives. I see no reason whatever for considering that this is a justifiable alteration of our fiscal policy in this country, and I should like very much to know just what effect the Minister of Finance considers this particular paragraph of the income tax resolutions will have on the revenue of the national government, if it is enacted.

I confess I was surprised and disappointed to hear one of my fellow members from British Columbia adopt an attitude of this kind, because I think if he understood the reason behind the introduction of this resolution he, as well as all hon. members of the committee, would support it. This is not an attempt, as I understand it, to give some special advantage to large corporations in the forest industry. Rather, and the minister can correct me if I am wrong, it is my understanding that the intention of this legislation is to correct an injustice, a discrimination, which has existed for a long time and which applies to all loggers not only in British Columbia but in the province of Ontario. Since 1949 in Ontario and since 1953 in British Columbia the forest industry in those two provinces has been burdened with income taxes which do not apply to the forest industries in any other part of Canada. Under the guise of resource taxes the two provinces in question have imposed what are in effect income taxes. If hon. members analyse the legislation in the two provinces they will see that the taxes are based on the profits which are made. The industry in both Ontario and British Columbia has been fighting these taxes on a united basis ever since they were imposed.
I would have thought that a member from a riding where the forest industry provides the principal means of livelihood would be fighting for the small man who is affected by these taxes-
On Vancouver island there are no small operators.

Well, in other parts of British Columbia, and certainly in Ontario, there are a lot of small operators and they have to pay income taxes ranging from 2 to 5 per cent higher than industry in general in all parts of Canada.
As a member from British Columbia I was somewhat disappointed that the remedy which is attempted by this resolution has been to some extent nipped in the bud by the government of British Columbia, which earlier this year put through legislation which was supposed to complement the resolution we are

considering. In so doing they held back a little, and as a result of this action discrimination will still continue in the province of British Columbia. As far as this side of the house is concerned we approve of this resolution, which is supported by the forest industries and the service industries associated with them, certainly in both British Columbia and Ontario.

I have listened to the remarks by my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands and by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. I think the hon. member missed the point of the criticism which was made by my hon. friend. What he is seeking is equality of treatment as between the large operators and the small operators in British Columbia, a state of affairs which has not existed to date, whether we are considering provincial taxation or federal taxation. What he was complaining about is the fact that those who are reaping without having sown, as it were, will be able to take advantage of this legislation while those who throughout the years have provided for an increase in our natural resource wealth will not be able to do so.
This is a question which has been under serious consideration by those who are interested in conservation and the development and ownership of private tree farms in Canada. When I say private tree farms I mean ownership in part of a farm or on a small scale, where a man is interested in spending his lifetime developing this forest capital. In that connection I think there is no question but that the present Income Tax Act militates against sound tree farming on the part of the small operator, and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands takes that stand with me.
I just want to quote, Mr. Chairman, a few paragraphs from "Forestry Tenures and Taxes in Canada", which is a report on a very extensive study made by the tax foundation of Canada. In this respect the report has this to say:
There are two income tax matters about which conservation groups, such as the conservation council of Ontario, are very concerned. One is that just discussed-the operation of the lure of making capital gain as an obstacle to the creation, preservation and good management of farm wood lots, plantations and tree farms. The other is the bar to deduction of losses incurred in the early years of a plantation from income from another source.
In brief, the interest of conservation groups and members of forestry societies is that land which is best employed as forest land should be kept continuously productive.
In this connection I might say that our income tax legislation and our property tax

legislation, as far as the provinces are concerned, make that almost impossible under certain circumstances.
There are social returns, in the form of protection of watersheds, wildlife and the recreational value of the woods above and beyond the monetary return to the owner.
That is a matter which is almost completely overlooked by specialists in taxation matters, who look purely at dollars and cents, papers and figures.
As well, farmers do not realize that a high rate of return can be secured from a properly managed wood lot, and the work of education is obstructed by tax considerations. Finally, since the social value of plantations and tree farms-
-and when we are talking of tree farms here we are talking of tree farms in the proper sense of the word, which have been planted by the owner, or cared for and brought into production by the owner over a long period of years.
-exceeds the private return to the owner, there is justification for tax provisions which make tree farming attractive, or at least do not act to thwart the intensive management of woodlands.
A specific complaint is that a farmer can charge off, as current costs of operating his farm, the expenses he incurs (other than his own labour) in starting a new wood lot or plantation.
Mr. Chairman, this is the complaint we are making, and we are making it because we want to contrast that with how the tree farmer is treated. We consider that the farmer should have this right. The report continues:
This is because it is not practicable to try to segregate the finances of the various parts of a farm's operations-all expenses and income are lumped together. On the other hand, if a hobby tree farmer buys a tract of timber land in poor condition and improves it greatly by afforestation of bare areas with a view to making it an intensively managed, continuously productive wood lot, his expenses in the early years when no income is produced may not be used to reduce his taxable income drawn from other sources.
That is the same as a farmer who would draw it from other sources in connection with agriculture.
The expenses of creating the plantation must be cumulated in a depletion account for claim when timber is cut decades later. Yet there is a net gain to the public above the return to the tree farmer himself.
Mr. Chairman, I do urge the minister to give consideration to this problem. I urge him, first of all, to consider treating all costs of establishing and maintaining a new plantation as current costs of operation. Second, I urge him to aggregate losses so calculated in the early years of establishing the plantation with income from other sources. And third, I urge him to include in the expenses so treated maintenance costs, annual property taxes, all planting costs, costs of protection from fire,
Income Tax Act
disease and insects, and of installations for improvement of the limit such as tile drainage, roads, and so on.
The great complaint of the small operators in my own district is this, and, I am talking of tree farmers who own the land and have tree farmed it for many years. They are not able to charge provincial taxes as a cost of operation. They are not able to charge cost of road building. They are not even able to charge forest protection tax. The members of this group urge that the minister give consideration to this problem so that at least the small tree farmer will receive the same consideration that is presently enjoyed by the larger operators, and I think that is a very fair presentation. In the opinion of this group, up to this time they have not enjoyed the same treatment; as the larger the operation, the greater is the opportunity to take advantage of various sections of the Income Tax Act and provincial legislation to charge off a cost of operation when computing income tax or other taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit me to intervene for one moment, we are now dealing with paragraph 6 but he has said he is going to deal with paragraphs 6 to 10. I want to tell him that I propose to move an amendment to paragraph 9 when we come to it, so he might bear that in mind.

That is fine. Resolutions 6 to 10 primarily affect the oil and gas industry in Canada. It was estimated by the previous minister when they were introduced that they will cost the treasury some $15 million in a full year. The oil and gas industry as such will contribute very little to the income tax revenue of the federal government even though its gross revenue exceeds $500 million. I can think of no other industry in Canada in this favourable position.
It has been claimed that this industry needs further encouragement to find reserves. According to figures produced by the Canadian petroleum association, at the end of 1961 reserves on hand in Canada amounted to 18.9 years supply. If we compare our situation with the United States we will find that the United States had on hand at the same date

some 12 years supply, and over the past 100 years the United States working inventory has ranged between 10 and 15 years. By this standard, Mr. Chairman, we have too much oil on hand. Similarly, in Venezuela we find that at the end of 1961 they had about 18 years proven supply on hand and like Canada they are producing at only about 50 per cent of their maximum capacity.
What we need is more and faster growing markets for petroleum products. If we had these we would not need tax concessions to stimulate the search for oil. It is noteworthy in this regard that we import far more oil than we export, in spite of our unused capacity, and this is a factor contributing to our exchange problems. Incidentally, although we have had a national oil program, according to bureau of statistics figures capital investment in oil producing was $561 million in 1961 compared with $697 million in 1957.
I would think the next thing to consider is, who is going to benefit from these tax concessions contained in resolutions 6 to 10? Foreign control and ownership of this industry has been increasing and this legislation, I submit, will do nothing to discourage foreign ownership and encourage Canadian ownership. In this particular type of industry you have to go into the business wholeheartedly and operate in a big way to make a success of oil and gas exploration and development. Permitting other Canadian interests and industries to dabble in this type of activity is no way to ensure the expansion of Canadian investment in this field.
Under the present government, foreign ownership of our oil and gas industry has continued to grow. To give some examples, Superior of California has taken over Calgary and Edmonton, Phillips has taken over Pacific Petroleum and very recently the Shell Oil Company has taken over Canadian Oil. Close to 90 per cent of the acreage and 85 per cent of the proven oil and gas reserves in western Canada are now in foreign hands. Thus, Mr. Chairman, the benefits from this legislation will go largely to foreign investors in this field rather than to Canadian citizens.
These measures were drafted about a year ago, Mr. Chairman. Since the time they were drafted, and perhaps this has something to do with the minister's proposed amendment, this industry has received a windfall as a result of devaluation. Its export earnings, together with some increases in domestic prices, have added between $10 and $15 million to its gross revenues at the wellhead. Why, Mr. Chairman, if this is the case does the industry need a further shot in the arm amounting to some $15 million?

I want to make it clear this resolution is designed to help exactly the people over whom my hon. friend was expressing some concern. It is designed basically, first of all, to encourage participation in the industry by more Canadians by giving them certain tax concessions. This is very clear in the resolution. Second, this measure offers Canadians an opportunity to compete on a favourable basis with their United States counterparts in the development of our own resources.
As I have said before, it is significant that this is exactly the resolution which was introduced in the previous budget and which met with unanimous support from the independent companies who will be the chief beneficiaries. The hon. gentleman asks who is going to benefit from this? First of all, it is going to provide a considerable benefit to Canadian companies by reason of the fact that it will encourage Canadians to participate more broadly in the industry. It is going to permit write-offs against the high expenditures of a high risk industry. These are factors which apparently are not generally understood when the hon. member says these are privileges that are offered to no other industry. No other industry, Mr. Chairman, has to encounter the risks that are involved in exploring for oil.
It is hoped this measure will encourage more development, Mr. Chairman, at a time when it is so necessary. Another point, of which the hon. gentleman seems to lose track when he makes certain comparisons on the basis of oil reserves in the ground and the rate of discovery, is that there is a great deal of concern throughout the free world over these same figures, that is the relationship of the known reserves to the rate of use. The rate of consumption is reaching desperate proportions. There is great concern in the petroleum industry over the lack of discovery of new oil fields. I can understand that the hon. member would not perhaps appreciate that one of the desires of all people associated with the industry in any way, shape or form-I am including those people directly concerned with it-is to find new oil fields. If this is not done then Canada, and in fact the whole free world, could in a few years find itself in the position of having a shortage of oil which would, indeed, be a very dangerous situation.
When we reach paragraph 9 I am going to ask the minister certain questions relating to interpretation, and perhaps his amendment will cover them. However, may I assure him that at least the majority of those people

who are concerned with the development of this industry, and in particular the Canadians who are involved in this industry, feel this resolution goes a long way toward removing some of the handicaps they have been faced with in competing with the United States companies. As against that, Mr. Chairman, members of this group have repeatedly urged that the same consideration be given to farmers if the desire is to increase production. Moreover, in the case of the farmer, because of the nature of his operations and the nature of the farming industry in general, the country is assured to a much greater extent that this type of legislation will not be abused if the farmer wishes to take advantage of it to increase his capital investment in productive land and thereby increase his income.
I urge the minister to give consideration to enunciating a policy that will permit the government to give some direction and make these companies accept some responsibility after receiving these favours with respect to income tax, and I also urge him to give the farmers the same consideration.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned for lunch I was speaking of the position of the oil industry in Canada and suggesting that it was in a sufficiently healthy condition and was already in receipt of generous allowances by the government so as not to warrant this rather sweeping amendment to the Income Tax Act which is before us, which would provide still further increments for that industry. I have some figures in this regard which I think might well be put upon the record, sir.
We could, for instance, put on the record the depletion allowances that are now paid both to corporations engaged in the oil industry and to individuals who hold shares in oil companies. The corporation itself is permitted to deduct 33J per cent of its total income from its capital income. The shareholder is permitted a 25 per cent dividend deduction from his taxes. With regard to the contribution to the treasury, I think it is as well that we should have some idea of the magnitude of this particular operation and see what the figures are even in the distressed circumstances, shall I say, of the last three years.
The net value of the production in this industry-that is, less the cost of fuel, electricity and process supplies-will be of interest to the committee. The latest figures I can get are for 1960, but I have them also for 1959 and 1958. In 1958 they amounted to $407.1 million; in 1959 to $438.4 million; in 1960 to $453.4 million. From that enormous productive value they contribute a very meagre amount to the over-all operations of our country, in spite of the fact that they have been receiving very handsome profits during

those years, which have been going up steadily since 1958. The figures are $101 million in 1959, $104 million in 1960, and $109 million in 1961. This suggests to me, as I think it should suggest to most hon. members of the committee, that this is an industry which does not need any particular help. We are told, of course, that they must be given some allowance for the possibility of dry holes. I suppose that is so, if one does not think about it too clearly; but we must realize that if they hit a dry hole, if they make nothing, they pay no income tax anyway. What is proposed by that argument is that the taxpayers of Canada should recompense them for their bad luck in not having found a producing well. I suppose that is a principle that could be carried all through industry, but it would have rather a disastrous effect on our economy if the taxpayers were asked to subsidize every bad guess of private enterprise.
What it really amounts to is that we are being asked to help subsidize an industry that is well able to carry on its own functions without subsidies from the public purse. I would hope this committee would reject this proposal to further increase the emoluments of this part of our economy and have, rather, some consideration for the rest of the population who are not fortunate enough to be shareholders or directors of oil companies.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take two or three minutes to discuss paragraph No. 6 of the ways and means resolutions which are before us at the present time, and to mention specifically the oil industry. I was indeed rather surprised before the luncheon adjournment to hear the comments of the hon. member for Kingston with respect to this resolution. I know, coming from the area that I do in Saskatchewan, that he would not endear himself to the hearts of those in the oil industry in that particular part of Canada, because a great number of them, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary South, are private enterprisers, small companies establishing themselves in Canada in this great industry.
To give the committee some information on the extent of the oil industry in our particular area, the last figures I had early this spring show that in Saskatchewan we had, I believe, 4,865 producing wells. I am very happy to say that over 3,000 of those are in the great riding of Moose Mountain. I know that the people in my area interested in this industry would want me to support the resolutions that have been introduced by the Minister of Finance. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I should like to support this resolution and I would

also reiterate the words of the hon. member for Calgary South, who has put this matter into proper perspective.
With reference to some of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Kootenay West, who was comparing the oil industry with the farming industry, I am sure afl hon. members of this committee are interested in the welfare of the farmer, and so am I, because that is also a great industry in our riding. But I do not think the comparison is as valid as was suggested, because the oil industry, as we know, is a great risk enterprise, whereas a man who is versed in the ways of farming can look at the topographical nature of the area in which he is going to set up business and see whether or not there is a risk involved. Due to the topographical nature of the area involved and through soil survey he is able to find out, through a soil survey, whether the land is suitable for profitable farming or not. However, this does not apply to the oil industry, as the hon. member knows and I do not think, therefore, that the illustration he gave was realistic. Speaking on behalf of my constituents, I wholly support the resolution being introduced by the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Chairman, maybe my name will become famous enough one day to have a constituency called after it, but not yet.
I would just like to address a couple of questions to the Minister of Finance. We are studying some changes in the law intended to help the gas companies in Canada, and I should like to know from the minister the amount of oil or gas we are importing into Canada. I should like also to know if the Canadian gas companies could obtain in Canada, particularly western Canada, the gas or oil which we are now importing from outside Canada. As my third and last question, I should like to ask the minister if he does not believe that by helping gas and oil companies to consume the raw materials which we can produce in this country, instead of importing them, it would assist them as much as the amendment we are studying today.

I wish to make a few brief observations because it has been suggested from two sides of this committee that the resolution provides more generous terms to the petroleum industry than to other segments within our economy. Earlier, I endeavoured to explain that what have been described as generous terms should be related to two factors-first, the risk of the operations involved and, second, the desirability of finding new reserves in Canada.
I have already indicated in this house that the search for oil is a highly speculative
Income Tax Act
business. Here are the most recent figures I have, drawn from a reputable publication called "Oil and Canada" for the period ending October 26th. Of a total of 57 wells drilled, 24 found oil, nine found gas and 24 were dry. So the people who drilled those wells had very little to show for a great deal of capital expended. In some instances, as I have already indicated, deep drilling costs more than $1 million a well.
The second point I wish to make is that for the first time in western Canada's oil history gross production income is forecast at about $710 million as against a net cash expenditure of approximately $600 million. This surplus, or expected surplus, of about $100 million should be measured against a deficit last year of about $74 million or, against a deficit of $2 billion in the last 15 years. So we can see that these explorations cost a great deal of money and a great loss to the industry itself. The improvement in the position this year can be attributed directly, I believe, to the policy of this government in, first of all, processing a number of gas applications-I have already put on record the result of this-and, second, by the development of a national oil policy. Oil production in 1958 amounted to 465,000 barrels. By the end of this year it will be well over 700,000 barrels. Thus the improvement in industry revenue.
One hon. member from the New Democratic party suggested that the depletion allowance which is granted the industry is in itself a generous provision. Unfortunately, the conditions under which this allowance was made available were such as to prohibit any company other than a fully integrated company from taking any advantage of it. It is for this reason that the Canadian independents- I emphasize the word "independents"-came to the government and asked for the introduction of legislation based on these regulations which would permit them to enjoy benefits already enjoyed by their United States counterparts.
Every known authority has expressed concern over the lack of oil discoveries in western Canada. I have many references to which I could draw the committee's attention, including statements by the staff engineers of the Alberta oil and gas conservation board whose duty it is to examine these matters. Estimates of the remaining recoverable reserves of oil are likely, they say, to amount to 6.2 million barrels at the end of 1970 and they see little likelihood of an increase after that period at the present rate. The board itself foresees a sharp decline in the Alberta reserves from a 22-year supply to a 12-year supply by 1975. It further said in its most recent report that it was not in the public

Income Tax Act
interest to have this index of probable future reserves fall below a 12-year period of supply. It was partly on this account that a permit was granted for the exploration of the Athabasca tar sands to supplement conventional production. Though this area has a fantastic estimated reserve of oil, no one knows how much is recoverable. An initial permit of 37,000 barrels has been authorized over a four-year period. It remains to be seen if it can be achieved.
My second authority for this revised view of Canadian reserves is an engineer well known throughout Canada, Mr. J. P. Lons-bury of the department of economic research of the Toronto-Dominion Bank. He said that Canadian reserves are at their lowest ratio since 1957 and though substantial additions were made last year they were all from fields presently known.
Next to reserves, capital is the commodity most urgently required in order to stimulate oil exploration. It is important that this capital should be developed in Canada and these regulations are designed basically to assist Canadians. Finally, the hon. member for Kootenay West expressed some concern that the petroleum industry in western Canada might be able to take advantage of these incentives and then cap their completed wells. This hardly seems logical. Such an action would not be within the control of a company. You only cap a well when it is an inefficient producer. This comes within the authority of the provincial regulatory bodies, not of the federal government or of individual companies.
Reference was also made to markets. One hon. member suggested that the proper solution is to foster additional markets and not to provide more incentives. Surely, that is in line with the development we have seen since the introduction of the national oil policy. It is true that at first the oil policy was largely dependant on exports to the United States, but we hope that with the development of new refinery capacity the time will come when these exports to the United States will decrease.
I suggest that these regulations are designed to achieve the ends the hon. member wants to see-new markets, and new opportunities for Canadian participation.
