speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is with reference to the remarks of the hon. member for York-Humber. While I was busy seeking citations to support-
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. This matter has been already disposed of. There is no need to bring the point up again; I thought I had dealt with it adequately.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to prolong discussion on paragraph 6, but I do want to say that in the opinion of our group this sets forth a very unsound basis for establishing taxation in this country. The two main arguments which have been advanced, particularly by the hon. member for Calgary South, are, first, that this is an industry which has a very high ratio of risk capital-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thought paragraph 6 was already carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will accept a certain amount of responsibility in that event. Perhaps I moved rather quickly after the point of privilege had been raised by the hon.
Income Tax Act
member for Calgary South and called "carried", but I do not want to hurry the committee unnecessarily, and we can revert to paragraph 6 if that is the wish of the committee. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I did want to speak to paragraph 6 at the time you called it, but I cannot blame you if you could not see me. I did want to say that the hon. member for Calgary South based his argument on two points. First of all, that this is an industry with a high ratio of risk capital, and some compensation should therefore be made in the form of writing off some of the losses in exploration and drilling against income tax. Second, he said that there is a great need in Canada for further exploration if we are going to meet the anticipated needs of the future.
With reference to the first point, I should like to say that it is undoubtedly true that this industry involves a high ratio of risk capital. I think it should also be recognized, however, that while the risk is great the returns are also very great, and that those who spend money looking for oil and gas, as for other minerals, receive a very generous return when they find them. They are allowed to develop and to use the resources which belong to all the people, and they are then going to dispose of the public domain for a royalty which is usually relatively small. The returns which have been made by the oil and gas industry over the years have been very substantial. It seems to me that to allow them to take what are legitimate expenses and legitimate risks, such as geological exploration and drilling, and to write them off against their taxes, is really to have the public treasury pay part of the cost of exploration and drilling.
Now, what will be the result of this? The hon. member for Calgary South and the hon. member for Moose Mountain say that this measure is to help the small companies. But if the small companies do not make a profit- and many of them do not-then, of course, this is of no benefit to them. This legislation will be of advantage only to those who have sufficient profits and are paying fairly high taxes; it will not help the small companies who are in the red. This legislation will help the large companies who have very considerable profits and who are able to charge part of their expenses off against the taxes which they would otherwise pay. As a matter of fact, the practice has grown up, particularly in the United States, that many of the large companies deliberately take part of their profits along with the write-offs which

Income Tax Act
they are allowed in order to do exploration work on projects which they had no intention of developing for many years, so that they have actually done exploration and preliminary work on projects far in advance and have done so largely at the expense of the public treasury. I submit that this is an advantage which is given to scarcely any other group in the community. In essence the public are paying for any unprofitable venture while the industry in question receives a very high return on those ventures which turn out to be successful.
The second argument is that we face the possibility of an oil shortage over a long period of years and therefore there is a great need for exploration and development. I agree that there is a very genuine concern about this matter and that there is need for exploration and development and for geological surveys. But it seems to me that if these companies want to get the long term benefit from the development of our natural resources they should be prepared to make that kind of investment. If the public treasury is going to be asked to make this kind of investment, then surely it should be done directly by the public treasury and, as we do now in some parts of the mining industry, let the federal government with the provincial governments do the kind of exploration work and the kind of geological surveys which we are now leaving to private companies. Then let those companies pay for the work that has been done when they come to carry out the actual development or exploitation of the resources in question. If the public treasury is going to pay the shot then the public treasury ought to get the benefit; but if industry wants to get the benefit, as it is getting now, then certainly it ought to pay the shot.
In my opinion paragraph 6 is simply the continuation of a handout from the public treasury to an industry which at the present time is doing quite well. I want to emphasize the point made by the hon. member for Kingston, that in the main the benefits of this provision will not go, as has been said, to Canadian companies. Ninety per cent of the petroleum industry today is in the hands of large American concerns and the benefit will go primarily to them and not to Canadian taxpayers or Canadian producers. I certainly hoped that some of the members of the official opposition, who have been so vociferous in so many other debates, would have given some support to the member for Kingston in opposing what I think is a very unsound principle of taxation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall paragraph 6 carry?
No, a standing vote, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: All those in favour of paragraph 6 please stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Who is calling a standing vote? If there is going to be a vote I should like to say a word or two before the debate is finished. The question of whether or not the federal government is subsidizing the industry is a matter for the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam and everyone else to decide for themselves, but the argument which has been advanced here is that this benefit is of no use to the small corporations because they cannot take advantage of it and is of advantage only to the large corporations. Having regard to the argument that has been raised, I would suggest that the large corporation is the one that is making a profit and the one which is paying income tax and so the large corporation is really in partnership with the Minister of National Revenue to the extent of 50 per cent or more of its earnings.
I am not trying to give a precis here or present a brief on behalf of the oil industry. Frankly I know very little about the oil industry except that I use gas in my car and oil in my furnace and I see pictures of oil wells all over western Canada. However, the argument that has been advanced that this provision is not going to help the little fellow who does not make any money but is going to help the big fellow who is paying a substantial amount of income tax is completely fallacious. I should point out that my predecessor and the government did not bring this legislation before the house last April at the request of any American corporation or at the request of any big corporation whatsoever. We brought it before the house and the committee, and I impress this on my friends who want a vote, at the request of the small independent oil operators. If my friends to my right, who are the friends of all the people, particularly the common people and the little people, want to vote against that, let them do so, but this legislation is for the benefit of the small operators and at their request. Otherwise it would not have been introduced.
It may be that there are areas in connection with its administration where there can be difficulties. I am not questioning the fact that some of the arguments raised may have a lot of merit, but I have given the background of this legislation and that is why we have this resolution before the committee at this time. I want members of the committee to understand that before they vote.

Mr. Chairman, this morning I spoke against the general principle of giving specific advantages in taxation to specific

Income Tax Act
industries, and I think there is much to be said for this as a principle of taxation. However, I do not think we can accomplish this by voting against a few resolutions which are only a part of sections 83 and 83A of the Income Tax Act. If we wipe out these resolutions we do not get away from the principle involved in those two broader sections of the Income Tax Act.
Mr. Chairman, before the vote is called I have a couple of questions I should like to pose to the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am afraid I misled the committee to some extent in calling for a vote and in order to clear up that point right away I should like to give my authority. Normally resolutions on taxation are considered as a whole and not voted upon one way or another paragraph by paragraph. I apologize to the committee for rising so quickly in response to the request for a vote from the members of the New Democratic party. My authority for not so doing is set out at pages 275 and 276 of the Journals of 1948 when the house decided that a vote on a paragraph of a budget resolution was not in order and this was subsequently confirmed. I would refer hon. members to Hansard for May 2, 1951, page 2627. I will throw the paragraph open for continuing discussion.

I should like to put a question to the minister that might clarify this whole picture a good deal. The minister has said that this provision was incorporated in the budget resolutions by his predecessor largely at the request of certain small oil companies. I know the minister would not say that that would be a compelling reason for putting it in because any group of taxpayers is very apt to ask for relief from taxation for that particular group. I assume that the minister's predecessor would have made some pretence of establishing that there was some national interest in doing so. That is what we should be concerned about in the committee. It is not whether a group of oil companies or even the hon. and passionate member for Calgary South think this is a good thing-
Thank you very much.

-but whether or not it is in the interests of Canada to have a special tax concession for this particular industry is a different matter. I think that if the minister or the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration who was the parliamentary secretary to the minister of finance at the time the budget was introduced, could explain to us in very simple language just what national interest is
served in making this special tax concession, which is the only reason why we should support it, I am sure that might help a great deal to get a more harmonious feeling in the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I certainly do not have to tell the hon. gentleman, who once sat on the treasury benches, that any minister of finance is under pressure to relax taxation and to give some concession to this group or that. I am sure this is something that my predecessors have gone through ever since confederation. I would not be betraying any secrets at the moment, Mr. Chairman, if I were to admit that the present minister may be going through somewhat the same pressures. The fact that one grants a concession, if it is a concession, must indicate something unusual, some argument, some motivation, rightly or wrongly, upon which the minister acted. The minister can make mistakes and governments can make mistakes. We all know that. However, no minister is going to succumb to pressure to relax taxation measures, because once he starts doing that he is in a hopeless situation and can no longer carry out his responsibilities as minister of finance.
Now, in the judgment of my predecessor in office and of the government of which I was a member and for which I take full responsibility, this measure was in the interests of Canada because it was necessary to assist the independents, it was necessary to encourage expansion and to develop greater reserves of oil over a period of years. As the hon. member for Calgary South said earlier today there is a time coming, fairly rapidly, when the world which moves on wheels will be short of oil. What was considered a surplus supply three or four years ago is now at a level where you can almost compute the end of it mathematically. You have to get cooperation to get more reserves than we have today.
I cannot document this, Mr. Chairman. I cannot give a mathematical calculation or anything of the kind, but I say to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that in the opinion of the government, of my predecessor and of the present Minister of Finance, this measure is desirable to further the development of the oil industry in Canada.

I think perhaps I might ask the minister one more question. It was suggested by several hon. members who spoke on this matter that this was really a tax concession almost exclusively to United States interests and not to Canadians. I think if the minister could give us a satisfactory and rather more concrete reply to that than his previous reply, it would help the committee a great deal.

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but I cannot give the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate statistics as to the proportion of Canadians vis-a-vis people of the United States who would benefit from this concession. All I can say to the hon. member, and to the committee, is that this concession was requested by Canadians, Canadian producers and by Canadian association representations that were made to the government, to me as minister of national revenue at that time and to my predecessor, the then minister of finance. This concession was given, therefore, in the interests of the Canadian industry. Although I cannot give the figures to the hon. member this afternoon, I presume that they would be available to some extent, Mr. Chairman, at the dominion bureau of statistics. When we get to the bill and we are considering it in committee, I will try to give to the hon. member the detailed information he has requested.

I thank the minister very much for that undertaking. I understand the minister will, in the committee stage on the bill, so far as possible show what the real extent of this may be and show, so far as he can, the benefit to both small and independent operators and above all to Canadians, whether small or large. This would be of great assistance to us in trying to frame tax legislation. What he is saying seems to be a sound, conservative conception at any rate, in that the minister does seem to be trying to conserve an industry, but we would like him to give a conservative base to his argument by giving some concrete evidence in this committee. I do think if that could be done a lot of us would feel a great deal easier about this whole matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will give whatever evidence is available and I will produce it when we are in the committee stage on the bill.

I should like to make a comment, partially in reply to the excitable hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. First of all, for his satisfaction, I should like to point out that these representations were not made by a group of small oil companies. They were made by industry associations in general. It is perhaps interesting to note, Mr. Chairman, that the industry asked for considerably more than they received. I agree with the government that the requests of the industry, had they been granted, would not have been to the benefit of the Canadian industry primarily. The industry request was related to gross depletion on production revenue which would have benefited the United States companies to a greater extent than the Canadian companies.

The former minister of finance has included three basic principles in this resolution which the minister has undertaken to explain in detail, so that even the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will see that they are going to benefit Canadians. This has been clearly established-
We are not at all satisfied with the sound conservative basis of the minister's explanation, even although the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was satisfied.
I am not satisfied yet, but we have been promised a more detailed explanation.

The hon. member came so close to satisfaction that I took it he was satisfied. From our reading of statistics generally before us we understand that some 90 per cent or more of the acreage in which some of this drilling and exploration will take place is now in the hands of United States controlled corporations. It is strange that, under our taxing system, every time some small business asks for a benefit it is the big fellows who really get it. We are not at all satisfied, therefore, that this is a proper principle.
I want to turn to another point. As a new member of this house, I am completely flabbergasted at your suggestion, Mr. Chairman, if I may say so with respect, that you cannot have a standing vote on the portion of the resolution before the committee. It seems every time we pass a paragraph you ask: Is this paragraph carried? May I respectfully suggest to you that when you ask that you are, in effect, making us vote. Surely, a paragraph can neither be carried nor rejected unless there has been a vote, whether the vote is by voice or by silence, as it is in most cases, or by standing. It is still a vote. In my innocence, inexperience and probably ignorance, I would have thought the only purpose of a standing vote as distinct from silence was to see what members vote which way and to have a more accurate count than you get by silence or by voice. Therefore I would be most grateful, Mr. Chairman, if you would explain to me how you can call something carried if there has not been a vote; and if it were not carried does that not imply there was a vote, and therefore why cannot that vote be taken by a standing vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member, as we all know, is a learned student who has read politics, history, philosophy and dogma, particularly dogma, for many years. He knows very well, Mr. Chairman, that when the resolution before the house is a budget resolution it is perfectly true what he says, that

as a matter of convenience the chairman deals with it paragraph after paragraph and he says "carried" because it is of convenience to hon. members to know whether we are on page four, page 41 or 44, or whether we are dealing with paragraph one or paragraph 91. Although I am not a constitutional authority, and I do not profess to be, I am convinced that the constitutional authority is that we have one budget resolution before the house.
That may be awkward. It may be inconvenient. You can move to strike it out but you cannot move to increase it because that would be contrary to our rules. You can move to delete something, but it is still one resolution, and although the chairman calls paragraph 1, paragraph 2, paragraph 3, paragraph 4, the tradition and background of this thing is that we have one resolution in front of us which we have to accept or reject.

I think, Mr. Chairman, I shall have to support the minister, hard as that is to do, upon this occasion because last Friday-I think it was last Friday-when we began to discuss this resolution and when the acting minister was piloting it he was very anxious to take each of the paragraphs separately, and I was very insistent that we should have a general debate on the whole resolution. I said there would have to be unanimous consent to take up the paragraphs separately because there was only one resolution before us and it had to be considered as a whole.
Having been sustained by the Chair over the mild objections of the treasury benches on one occasion, I feel I could not possibly argue in the opposite sense now, and the precedents that Your Honour cited are those that are in the recollection of some of the older hon. members of the house, and in my recollection too, although I was not a member of the house at that time. I do not think there is any doubt that what the minister said is the correct procedure.
Why do we vote on one paragraph and not on the others?
Mr. Chairman, I do not suppose you would allow me to give the hon. member for York South a lecture on procedure, particularly when the greatest professor on the subject is right behind him.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it would be useful for the house to consider for a moment how we got to this position. I refer to the position which you have taken on the basis of the citation that you quoted a moment ago.
Income Tax Act
Prior to 1948 these income tax resolutions were dealt with one by one. I was here at that time, as were other hon. members now present. Incidentally we were debating in 1948 certain tax changes that had been brought in by radio, but nevertheless the house was being given the opportunity to confirm them afterwards. We were dealing with them in committee of ways and means. The particular resolution before us had to do with increasing taxes on stoves, refrigerators, washing machines and things of that sort, and the point was reached when we who sat on the opposition side of the house-we were Conservatives, C.C.F.'ers and Social Crediters in opposition in those days-outnumbered the Liberals who were sitting on the government side of the house. We called a vote, a standing vote, as my colleague from York South sought to call one a moment ago.
Mr. William Golding was in the chair as deputy chairman of committees of the whole. The vote was taken by a standing vote and we on the opposition side of the house won the vote. The resolution to increase taxation was defeated.
Mr. Abbott was then minister of finance. He started to do what I thought was the correct thing, to ask that the committee rise so that the government could consider what to do, having lost its resolution in the committee; but he immediately got advice from a colleague, the late Ian Mackenzie who suggested he try some other course. That other course was to challenge the holding of the vote that had just been taken. A long procedural debate ensued, in which the Liberals argued that the chairman had no right to put the vote on one of the paragraphs of the income tax resolution.
That proposition was fought bitterly by the Conservatives. I was in the fight too, but that would not be any surprise, and so were the Social Crediters. Mr. Golding stood firm. He said it was in order to have taken the vote, the vote had been taken and the resolution had been defeated. In the face of Mr. Golding's firm stand, and I may mention Mr. Golding was a Liberal and the Liberals were in power, Mr. Abbott appealed that ruling to the house.
Mr. Speaker was called in to put the vote to the house. The bells were rung and the Liberals were brought in and the ruling of the deputy chairman, Mr. Golding, was upset. That is how we got into this situation, it was because the Liberals of that day did not like being beaten in committee of ways and means.
I contend, Mr. Chairman, that that was a wrong decision of the house, that the ruling of Mr. Golding in the chair was a correct one, and that we should get away from that ridiculous position that you have to vote on 10

Income Tax Act
or 15 propositions that are different and that are in one resolution, instead of taking them one by one as we did prior to that occasion in 1948.
In that connection, Mr. Chairman, even if one persists in standing by the decision made by a Liberal house, opposed by the Conservatives of that day, I remind you of what it says at page 298 of Bourinot's fourth edition:
A motion which contains two or more distinct propositions may be divided so that the sense of the house may be taken on each separately.
I submit that the resolution before the committee has 15 distinct propositions, so distinct, Mr. Chairman that a moment ago you had to get unanimous consent to go back and discuss one that had been carried. There are 15 distinct propositions, and if you feel you are bound by that house vote in 1948, I submit you should have consideration for the sentence I have just read from Bourinot's fourth edition:
A motion which contains two or more distinct propositions may be divided so that the sense of the house may be taken on each separately.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that is precisely what you have been doing, and that the member for York South is right. At the end of the consideration of each paragraph you have said "Is section so and so carried?" There has been some murmur of "carried," and you have moved on to the next section. You have in effect been taking the sense of the house on each proposition separately. It is easy to take the sense of the house when there is no division. You take silence to be consent, and go on; but if the house is divided on a proposition and the committee has different views, surely the only way to take the sense of the house is by the method of a vote.
As my leader points out, if that is not the case, if we are not taking them one by one, then how can you have order and what is to stop hon. members jumping from paragraph 2 to paragraph 13 and back again to paragraph 6? We are taking them in an orderly fashion, one by one, getting the sense of the committee in each case.
I said to my colleague from York South a moment ago when you, sir, began to put the question, "This is a very happy day for me. My good friend, who happens to be my member in this House of Commons, considering where I live in Winnipeg, is wiping out a 14-year injustice". But I find that I have a complaint to register against my member. You are retaining the injustice. Therefore, just as I did not vote for you, sir, last June 18, I will not vote for you next time either.

I might say, Mr. Chairman, that on the same page of Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, there is another paragraph which says, with regard to complicated questions, that it is always open to a member to move formally that a question be divided. Admittedly there are two types of these multiple things; one is called a complicated question and the other is a motion which contains two or more distinct propositions. I do not think this is merely a complicated question, in which case a member should move for it to be divided. I think this is clearly a motion that has 15 distinct propositions and that you, sir, should have regard to common sense; you should have regard to the practice up to 1948; you should have regard to the ruling of chairman William Golding; you should have regard to the position the Conservatives took on that occasion, and agree that this 15-point resolution that is before us contains 15 different propositions, and that the sense of the committee can and should be taken on them separately.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word on that point. I am not going to argue the historical question that the hon. gentleman raised. I was not in the house at the time, but my friends in the house took exactly the position I am taking now, just as the hon. gentleman took the position he is taking now. They were sustained by the house, and the hon. gentleman was not. This committee made a decision on this particular point last Friday. Whatever may be the usual practice or whatever should be the proper practice, I was very insistent last Friday, over the objection of the acting minister, that we should take this resolution as one resolution. I actually said:
Of course, the Chair realizes that, on a strict point of order, it is one resolution that is before the committee and it can only be restricted by unanimous consent.
That consent was tacitly given; in fact, it was more than tacitly given, because we did have a short, general debate. Then there was agreement on this question. In fact, I was out of the chamber for a moment and when I came back I said, "Has there been unanimous consent now to take up the paragraphs one by one?" That was done as a matter of convenience; but it was clearly recognized-and the committee, of course, is master of its own procedure, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre well knows-that the objection should have been taken at that time and the point of order raised at that time.
Mr. Chairman, could I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.
What page of Hansard was the hon. member reading from?

I was reading from page 1244 of Hansard for last Friday, when a precisely similar question came up and a decision was made by the committee and the Chair on this subject. The acting minister reluctantly proceeded to a general debate on the whole resolution, and then there was agreement, for convenience, to discuss it paragraph by paragraph. But there was no thought that each paragraph would be adopted separately, because we had insisted that under the rules the whole thing had to be adopted together.
Having taken that position, having insisted upon that rule being followed in committee, and there having been no objection taken, it seems to me that we cannot change that now, sir, so far as this resolution is concerned. If, when we come to the next resolution, the hon. gentleman wishes to raise the point of order and appeal to the house, or do anything of that sort to try to get the ruling reversed, that is another matter. But the committee made a decision last Friday on this precise point, and I maintain, sir, that we should proceed with the decision we then made.
Mr. Chairman, to assist the hon. members, I do not think it would be of value to this committee to take up more time and I withdraw my request for a standing vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would just like to add one point to the very learned discussion we have had, contributed to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I wonder whether he has considered this fact. Although he was quoting from Bourinot with regard to a motion which might be divided into two or more distinct propositions, we are here dealing with a resolution, and a resolution is brought into the house and is followed by a bill. If the hon. member will look at the order paper he will find several resolutions there which contain several propositions; but the resolutions are written as a paragraph, divided by semicolons. It appears to me from a consideration of this matter that the budget resolutions are, for the convenience of the house, divided and numbered, rather than written all in one distinct paragraph with just the separation of a semicolon. Rather than being a whole series of distinct propositions, it is a resolution, just as other resolutions are, on which subsequently a bill will be founded and in which distinct measures are brought forward. That is perhaps a portion of the argument that was overlooked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he was speaking on this matter.
Income Tax Act

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I just ask that you, sir, and the house leader consider this one further question. I refer you to page 1248 of Hansard for last Friday, after this discussion took place to which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate referred. In the middle of column 1 there appears this line:

Shall paragraph 1 carry? Paragraphs 1 and 2 agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am very glad that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre disclosed his franchise, because it helps me to be all the more impartial. I am going to be brief in my reference to this point of order, simply to co-operate with the hon. member for York South who said that he will withdraw his request for a division. While I rose perhaps instinctively, on the suggestion that there be a division on a section, I realize that I moved in haste and overlooked the authorities in support of the point of view I am now making, namely that there should not be paragraph by paragraph division.
My authority for that, briefly, is May's sixteenth edition, pages 411 and 412. Perhaps I might read a very brief portion of this passage on page 412 which is helpful to us:
The house does not recognize the right of individual members to insist on the division of motions moved in committee of the whole house, or of motions giving special facilities for the transaction of public business-
This is what I think we have done here. I say that as an aside:
-although it has sometimes agreed to do so on the appeal of an individual member.
Then there is a reference to where that occurred before, and I will not look that up at the moment. My other authority is one in which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has a particular interest. It was not in 1948, but in 1951 in Hansard, volume III, starting at column 1 of page 2627, where there is a very lengthy ruling by the then chairman which hon. members might look at in the interim period between the consideration of this resolution and the resolution which follows.
Shall paragraph 6 carry?

Carried.
No.

speechtext:
That paragraph 9 of the Income Tax Act resolution be deleted and the following substituted therefor:

Mr. Chairman, although I am speaking from this exalted position on the front bench, perhaps I should make it clear that the opinions I express are entirely my own.

These resolutions, like resolutions 6 and 10, are designed to aid the petroleum and mining industries. However, I would like to point out that, unlike the preceding resolutions, they allow a taxpayer, in this case a joint exploration corporation, to renounce expenses in favour of shareholder corporations, and in such circumstances, permit the shareholder corporations to deduct these expenses from their taxable income, providing the shareholder corporation carries on a business which could, in the circumstances, be deemed to be related to that of the joint exploration corporation. Indeed, resolution 12 when combined with resolution 10, goes so far as to permit a second successor corporation to deduct expenses incurred by the original corporation in drilling and exploration.
Mr. Chairman, when our taxation legislation is designed to favour certain specific industries or individuals, it necessarily leads to many complications. An examination of sections 83 and 83A of the Income Tax Act, with their numerous provisions, allowances and prohibitions, indicates the complexity of legislation which can develop from efforts such as these. As I have said before, I believe we should encourage Canadians to invest in the development of this heritage. I do feel that we must be careful in the extension of specific taxation advantages to non-resident ownership in this field. The government of Canada has to raise sufficient revenue through taxation to operate and carry out its social programs, and if specific taxation advantages beyond those enjoyed by Canadians generally are extended to citizens of other countries, it means that the Canadian taxpayer must make up for the lost revenue through higher taxes.
I should once again like to ask the minister whether he would indicate which corporations will benefit from these two resolutions. While I realize that it might not be wise to name specific companies, I do think he should indicate in a general way, based upon the analysis which must have been carried out prior to introducing these resolutions, whether or not the main benefit from these two particular resolutions will accrue to Canadians or to foreign-controlled corporations.
Another point which 1 should like to hear him discuss is whether or not he believes that it is furthering a dangerous precedent by allowing taxpayers to deduct from income expenses which were not directly incurred by them. Although there may be no particular danger in this regard in these two resolutions, if one accepted this as a general principle in our taxation system it could result in many abuses which would be unacceptable to the hon. members of this committee and to the Canadian public. For example, I can think of many corporate taxpayers operating in other 27507-3-94

I would request the minister to explain to the committee in some detail how the appropriate share is in fact to be determined.

Mr. Chairman, this resolution, which will result in an amendment or an addition to section HOB of the Income Tax Act, represents to my mind a reversal in thinking on the part of this government between 1961 and 1962. We all remember how the former minister of finance was, in 1960 and 1961, telling the Canadian people and foreign investors that the flow of capital into Canada must be stopped. The present government through its actions, including the introduction of section 11 OB into the Income Tax Act, was creating the impression abroad among foreign investors that the Canadian government was trying to find ways to discourage their participation in the development of the Canadian economy. This campaign proved very successful. In fact, it was so successful that the inflow of capital into Canada dried up entirely by June, 1962, and indeed there was a net capital outflow. This resulted in our government having to go hat in hand to the international monetary fund and to American and British central banks to borrow foreign exchange. It has been interesting to note, Mr. Chairman, that in this session there has been no expressed government antagonism toward foreign investors and indeed, as I have previously pointed out, the budget resolutions, including this present resolution, tend to favour foreign investors.
I have no doubt in my mind that this government is presently considering further legislation to encourage foreign investment in Canada. In fact, the increase in interest

rates which they have brought about certainly is not meant to benefit the internal growth of the Canadian economy, but rather to attract foreign investment into our country regardless of the effect upon Canadian expansion from within and the increase in job opportunities which would result therefrom. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that this resolution is intended to favour a relatively small number of foreign taxpayers and I question its advisability on these grounds. I would appreciate it if the minister would point out to this committee exactly whom it is going to benefit.
I sincerely hope, Mr. Chairman, that we will soon have reason to conclude that the government has become aware that there are other ways to control our destiny than by destroying the confidence of our friends in the government of this country. We must, Mr. Chairman, find ways-and the next Liberal government will find ways-of returning the control of our natural wealth to Canadians while, at the same time, assuring foreign investors that they will be fairly treated by our government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in the calm and peaceful atmosphere which is predominating here right now, I am sure that I should not reply in any way, but I must reply to some of the more or less specious arguments which my hon. friend has brought forward. The amendments of 1960 were not designed to discourage foreign investment, but they were designed to remove certain special privileges to foreign investors. Without going into an argument about the merits of them for the moment-my hon. friend, I know, with his skill and professional experience realizes that as much as I do-and without repeating the timing and merits of them, I would say that the legislation was justified at the time, and I will not go into any further details with respect to the events which happened in June. I certainly do not admit for one moment that anyone went with hat in hand or anything of the kind but, as I said, I think we had better not spoil the peaceful atmosphere this afternoon by reviving the debate. The fact remains that companies carrying on mining require tremendous investment of capital. We have had examples, of course, in northern Quebec, in northern Ontario and in the west, and it is obviously desirable that they should be able to carry on their business in the way suggested here and should be freed from this charge which was placed upon them by the original legislation. This is to help only the mining companies referred to in the section and I think it will serve a useful purpose and will help to develop the Canadian economy.

I should like to say a few words on paragraph No. 13. We note that it is for the purpose of bringing foreign capital into Canada to develop our natural resources, including mines. I must say I disagree completely with the Minister of Finance so far as that point of view is concerned. If we need capital to develop our natural resources in Canada we do not need to get the money from strangers in Chicago, New York, Vienna or anywhere else in the world.
We have here in Canada our own central bank, the Bank of Canada, and we should give consideration to using the Bank of Canada to create the capital to develop our natural resources. Then we will not need money from outside of Canada.
Second, I also disagree because, as I understood, the purpose is to help the austerity program and to find money outside of Canada to equilibrate our foreign reserves. In the past we have seen such laws enacted and they have not been done away with when the austerity program has ended. They will continue and those who will continue to benefit from the tax deductions will not be Canadian citizens but foreign corporations or companies. If we want to exempt such capital from taxation we must begin first by giving tax deductions to our citizens here in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I say one word on that point. There are many tax deductions for Canadian citizens at the moment. There are many tax deductions in the mining industry. This government feels, and I think the country generally feels, that it is advisable and necessary to have an inflow of capital into this country, and I hope that will continue indefinitely. Certainly when you look at the tremendous expenditures that have been made in the province of Quebec, in Labrador, British Columbia and Ontario you realize that the capital was not available in this country at that time with which to make those expenditures. Whatever one's views may be as to how capital can be engendered and developed, we feel that in this particular industry, which means so much to the Canadian economy and which requires such terrific sums of money running into hundreds of millions of dollars in some cases, provision such as this should be made to encourage the industry, and that is why it is being made.

In answer to what the
Minister of Finance has just said regarding the need of foreign capital in Canada to develop our own country, I should like him to remember that not so many years ago, possibly not so many months ago, he and the government were complaining about the effect 27507-3-944
Income Tax Act
on the stability of our foreign reserves of profits going out of Canada to other countries. They were complaining about profits from foreign capital invested here going out of Canada. If we continue such a system we will still be complaining about it in a couple of years and we will have the same kind of crisis as we had last June and will be obliged to keep Canada on an austerity program.

Am I correct in understanding that this exemption from paying the 15 per cent tax levied on non-resident corporations is now going to be granted to iron ore mining companies and only to iron ore mining companies?

If it is not a good thing, then we ought to wipe it out. My own feeling is that it is probably a good thing to have a tax on non-resident corporations.
I agree with what some of my friends across the way have said about the need for generating more capital in Canada. He said: Mr. Speaker, as I have looked through Hansard for the past few years I have noticed that this matter has been before parliament on several previous occasions and I apologize to those in the house who were members of parliament at that time for making statements which they will have heard several times previously. It is our view that the developments in recent years in Canada, as in many other democracies, have been such as to justify, indeed to require, that the voting age be reduced from 21 to 18.
I want to put forward first a proposition with which I am sure every member of the house agrees, that citizenship in a community does not really mean very much to the residents in the community until they have to do something about it. General propositions about freedom, democracy and liberty are not very useful or very meaningful to those who do not enjoy the fruits and the rights of citizenship, freedom and liberty. Our children in the schools are taught these things with an eye to the day when they will have an opportunity to enjoy the benefits of a free society such as we in Canada are proud to have.
Therefore I suggest, as a first proposition, that the vote ought to be given to our people at the first reasonable opportunity, at the first opportunity, that is to say, when looking at the situation as a whole one may reasonably conclude that the young people have had the kind of experience, the kind of training and the kind of environmental influences which will enable them to understand the meaning of the vote and to vote at least with the intelligence that we adults

do. I would expect that they might even do a great deal better than we do, but at least with that intelligence.
The reason for suggesting 18, as I see it, is that it is by and large, with exceptions, of course, the age at which in most parts of Canada our young people finish their secondary schooling and are either absorbed in the work force, if there is work for them or, if they are fortunate enough, go on to university for higher learning. In other words, it is by and large across Canada a very logical dividing line between adolescence and maturity for those of us who are fortunate enough ever to gain maturity and therefore it is a logical dividing line between the "kids" who are not to vote and the men and women who are to have the vote.
If we look around us we find that in various important aspects a person 18 years old is asked to assume some very real responsibilities for the society in which he lives and which has given him his education and, I hope, adequate opportunity. We must take every step available to us to improve their workings. We must make them alive in the minds and hearts of the people of our community. Recently, we were told that about 90 per cent of the Canadian people are reached by television.
Young Canadians know more about the election which took place a few days ago in the United States than older people knew of Canadian problems and affairs in days gone by. Greater facilities in education and better communications have given the younger people a large share of knowledge, and in Canadian universities the young people of today know more about Canadian political problems than their forefathers did at the same age.
The main problem is to find out what age group would be best suited. The evidence is voluminous that many people of 18 years and under are engaged in occupations, pay large amounts in taxes and do things to help the productivity of the country. Therefore they should be given the right to choose those whom they wish to be in charge of our political affairs.
Reference has been made to the age at which soldiers are taken into the army. We know soldiers are given a vote; but the younger soldiers, who may possibly be the first to be called upon to defend our nation, should also be given the right to decide the people they want in charge of the country's affairs.
I recall, when amendments to the election act were brought before the house a couple of years ago, the Prime Minister made a statement to the effect that the matter should be studied by a special committee at a later date and, speaking from memory, I believe he said hon. members of the house would be given the opportunity to make that study. The time has arrived for it to be undertaken, and it would be beneficial if the government did something to assist hon. members in undertaking the study that was contemplated.
During that debate references were also made to the effect that we should wait until the census returns were completed, but all the census returns will tell us would be the number of people in Canada between the ages of 18 and 21. A census could not in any way be a factor in determining at what age people should be given the vote, or in determining why the age of 18 would be better than any other age.

The Liberal party on many occasions has expressed its desire that a complete study be undertaken into the question of granting the franchise at 18 years of age instead of 21. Two years ago the then hon. member for Beauce, had a bill on the order paper similar to the one now under discussion. The hon. member for Skeena also had a similar bill which was discussed at that time, and I express the views of the Liberal party when I say we are prepared to make a complete study of this matter to see if the qualifying age could be lowered.
I have listened carefully to the hon. member for York South but I do not fully agree he has found all the reasons why 18 years would be the proper age. However I am prepared to state I have the same view, and I would be most happy if the Prime Minister would see fit to introduce a measure providing for the establishment of a special committee to study this problem, and to see that more complete information would be given that committee than was given the house in an indirect way a couple of years ago.
Certainly in the institutions of higher learning, as has been pointed out, some of the teachers are under 21 years of age, and doubtless they study political science. They have a great knowledge of the possibilities and needs of Canada and should have the right to go to the polls and choose their own representatives. If the committee decided that 18 years is the age at which the greatest number of Canadians become capable of exercising the franchise, then people of 18 years of age should be entitled to vote.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE AGE OF VOTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that this debate on the bill moved by the hon. member for York South should come up in this particular week which has been dedicated by a number of people in Canada as youth appreciation week. Thus it is singularly appropriate that the subject should be discussed this week.
As two previous speakers have pointed out, this is an old subject in the house and I would agree that it is a non-partisan one. I also think it might be safe to say that most hon. members, like most Canadians, do not have any very strong feelings one way or the other on the subject. Speaking for myself I know that if anybody could present me with a really good reason why we should lower the voting age to 18 then I would be quite in favour of it. On the other hand, I do not feel we should make change just for change's sake because sometimes our institutions, and I think one might describe the voting age of 21 as being an institution in
Canada Elections Act
our society, albeit a small one, have developed over the years as a result of experience.
Having said that, I would like to add that there are certainly many arguments both ways. In years gone by I have had some rather active experience with young people in one political party; I have even had association from time to time with people who were formally enrolled in other political parties, and I can say I have never really found any very strong demand among young people to have the voting age lowered from 21 to 18 although, to be perfectly fair, I have heard the subject discussed favourably among such groups.
We must look at some of the arguments on the subject, both pro and con. In the first place, Mr. Speaker, let us look at the arguments which are in favour of lowering the voting age to 18. It has been pointed out by some that, since young people have a much greater stake, from the long range point of view, in the future of the country, it would be advantageous to lower the voting age from 21 to 18. It is said that those who are 18 are naturally going to live longer and have a greater interest in what is going to take place in the country in the future. I think that is a pretty good argument. Another argument-and I think this was at least alluded to by the hon. member for York South is that it would help young people, even those at school, to develop an interest in our democratic way of life; it would be a great help in developing an interest perhaps to a greater extent than people have today. Again, I think that is a good point and one which deserves consideration. Likewise, the arguments that were put forward by the hon. member for York South are, I think, very good arguments. I would not in any way disagree with them, except one, and I will come to that in a moment.
Let us for a moment look at some of the arguments on the other side of this question. It has been said by some that at the age of 21 people have reached a greater degree of maturity than they have at 18. This, of course, is a matter of opinion. I agree that 21 is a purely arbitrary age which has been arrived at, but again-as I mentioned earlier-it has been arrived at over the years as a result of experience and for no other reason. It is quite true that some people are quite mature enough to vote at, perhaps, the age of 15; and, indeed, as was pointed out by the hon. member for York South, some people perhaps never reach sufficient maturity to vote at any age. But we cannot take extreme examples one way or the other. When we are dealing with large numbers of people who make up

Canada Elections Act
a community, or indeed a country in this case, we have to look at the average, if there is such a thing. Experience appears to have shown that 21 is the age when a greater degree of maturity is reached, rather than 18. Again, Mr. Speaker, if some can show me differently I will be quite willing to change my mind.
The next argument put forward-and I am not too sure that this is as valid an argument as some others-against lowering the voting age is that a citizen must be fully qualified in order to vote, and must be under no disability of any kind. Of course, as we know in Canada, this being a federal state with divided powers, we do not have the entire say in this house as to what legal disabilities people may be under. Some of these things are provincial matters. As we all know, until a person is 21 years of age he cannot own property, except under certain special conditions; he cannot enter into contracts, except under very special conditions; and indeed he is not responsible for his torts or wrongdoings except, again, in very special instances.
Some point out that right from the days of Pericles' Athens one of the qualifications for a person being allowed to vote, as far as being an Athenian citizen was concerned, was that he had to be fully qualified and under no disability. Until a person is 21 years of age, in Canada he is under those legal disabilities or disqualifications, if you want to put it that way. This is unfortunate, perhaps, but it is something about which we in this house cannot do anything. However, I do point out that this is perhaps not as valid an argument as some others. It is perhaps a more theoretical than practical argument.
The last point I would like to make against lowering the voting age concerns the question of our present society. I agree with the hon. member for York South that, as society changes, so our institutions must change with it. I fully agree with this. The hon. member for York South pointed out, I believe, that nowadays younger people have a greater opportunity of finding out what are the political problems of the day. He also pointed out that the age of 18 is perhaps a good, arbitrary dividing point since that is the time when some people go to work and others go on to university or some other form of higher learning. I think on this point that he and I would disagree. I feel that because of conditions which have developed over recent years in our society and show every indication, I hope, of continuing, perhaps there would have been a greater argument for lowering the voting age 20 years ago than there is today. Hon. members may wonder why I say this. I say it for this reason. In our modem society there is a much greater tendency to keep people at

school longer. There are government scholarships of various kinds, scholarships put up by organizations and the like, and training programs both federal and provincial which encourage people to stay at school longer. We hope they will stay at school longer, because in our complex industrial society people without skills are pretty well lost. I think that would be accepted as a fact by everyone.
For this reason there is a greater tendency for people-and I hope this will continue to be the case-to stay at school longer and take further training. For this reason I say that the voting age should remain at 21, because I think most people will agree that in order to participate in government one should have reached maturity. Maturity does not just mean reaching a certain physical age; it also means acquiring of experience. I do not think a person is fully experienced until he has left his academic training, or technical training, as the case may be, and has gone out into the world and had some maturing, practical experiences in the outside world. When one is attending school one is usually supported, to a degree at least, by one's parents, by the state, by the community or by some organization. Until one actually gets out and works in the world and, if I may put it this way, has knocked about a bit-

The hon. member for Kootenay East makes some observation about this. Perhaps he will deal with that later. Until one has this experience I do not think he can be considered mature. I think experience does a great deal in helping a young person acquire better judgment and discernment on various issues, rather than a purely academic background. I think there is something that should be considered in this respect. In this regard many people point out that when one is out in the world working, he has an actual stake in the community itself. You are helping to make your own living there; you are helping, by paying taxes, in the upkeep and maintenance of the community. When you have rather more practical experience in this regard, perhaps it helps one's discernment and judgment. I do not think one can go too far in this respect, but I believe it does help to some degree at least.
There are, of course, many arguments on both sides. I have tried to point out one or two in favour of lowering the voting age to which the hon. member for York South did not refer. However, there are those arguments against, which should be carefully considered. Like the two hon. members who have already spoken in this debate, I would

think that at some time a committee might well look into this matter, because it is a subject that has many facets. I do not think it is a matter of great urgency in making a change, whether it be to 18, 19, or whether the age should be raised, although I do not think I would really agree with that. But this question deserves very careful consideration. I know, Mr. Speaker, that there are other hon. members who wish to speak on this subject. I know one hon. member of the Social Credit party wishes to say something about this question, and there are others; therefore I will not take up any more time of the house.

I also assure him that I have no intention of killing his bill, I had prepared a somewhat longer contribution but I will make only a few remarks, to show him that I mean what I say. The proposal of lowering the voting age to 18 is certainly most sensible and had already been submitted to our convention in 1921. Long before our party was organized, we were already in favour of such an idea.
A few moments ago, the hon. member stated we had accepted some of his ideas. On the other hand, he also said that there might be differences of opinion and they should be given serious consideration. One has to split hairs like he does to be able to say that, while he is not against, he is not in favour, and that, while he is not in favour, he is not against, without ever saying why he is against.
I feel that if young people from 18 to 21 are bright enough and old enough to go to war and fight for us, they are also old enough to be entitled to vote.
I would ask the hon. member who spoke before me what he thinks of the great principle "no taxation without representation". If young people of 18 and over pay taxes to municipal, provincial and federal governments, what becomes of that principle when they are denied the right to vote?
Such discrimination should be wiped out as soon as possible. It is not possible to deny them the right to have their say in the administration of the country; they must be permitted to exercise their right to vote as they wish exactly as they have the right to order their own future.

We have the responsibility to prepare the future for our youth but I think it would be fair and logical that they could have something to say about it. One might think that I am preaching for my own party when I say that the young people generally accept new ideas. I should like an opportunity on behalf of my party to make a few brief observations on this subject. I see the time is getting close to a quarter to six, so I shall be very brief.
It seems that the action which is anticipated in this legislation gives formal recognition to the added burden which we are placing on our young men and women in today's society and of the role we shall expect them to play in the future. It takes into account the economic areas and the professions in which they are now participating while under the age of 21. I am referring particularly to the areas of teaching, service in the armed forces, with the police and in executive positions. I think it is appropriate that we should pass legislation today of the type suggested.
Almost all of us would agree, I believe, that heavy burdens will be placed on the shoulders of our young men and women in the years ahead and that if the cold war continues we shall expect them to take a more active role in confronting these difficulties than many of us have taken. In the light of this expectation it does seem reasonable that legislation such as we have before us should be passed.
I should like to comment briefly on some of the arguments which have been introduced, or referred to, as being unfavourable to this measure. I think they can be completely answered by reference to our expanding educational facilities and the great degree to which our young people are now taking advantage of them. This is virtually a day of mass education and the old arguments against young men and women having the vote are outmoded in the light of this consideration. Their awareness of the world situation has been sharpened because of the degree to which mass communications media have developed in this country, as they have in

This, I submit, makes young men and women far more competent to pass a judgment on the events of the day. Indeed, I believe they are just as competent to do so as our older men and women in Canada; they may be even more competent, because our young men and women today are very serious and concerned about the important questions which need to be resolved. They realize, perhaps, that they have many more years ahead of them than some of our older citizens and that it behoves them to have a considerable say in the policies which will determine their future.
I should like to make one or two comments on what was said by the hon. member for York South. I cannot help but wonder whether, as one of the leading spokesmen for the New Democratic party, he has tended to discount an increasing tendency on the part of young people to indicate their disenchantment with socialist dogmas and the old concepts of class society. Perhaps he has tended to discount the fact that young people today are prepared to accept the challenge of expressing their ideas within a party framework composed of people of different and varied interests; they express their views within that framework, but those views are tempered by the opinions of others. I wonder, also, if the hon. member has not ignored the tendency of our young people to be impatient when they see the frustration from which the country suffers by reason of the existence of minority groups. If he has given consideration to these matters, then I must say I admire the hon. member for his broadmindedness in being the author of the bill before us.
In conclusion, I think probably the greatest ancillary advantage which will arise if we enact this type of legislation in Canada is that increased impetus will be given to the necessity for the achievement of further advances in education by all levels of government. I think this will probably be the first demand of this new segment of our voters, if given the franchise. I think this would be a definite contribution to the good of Canada, and one which we all should welcome.

Mr. Speaker, I know time is getting on, but in order to relieve the anxiety of my colleagues in the house as to the necessity of having a vote on this bill tonight, I should start out by saying that I am not at all sure that I am ready for a vote on it. I am not sure that the house is ready to vote because

the question is one of those subjects on which it is very difficult to make up one's mind. I agree with many speakers who preceded me who said that the voting age, whether it is 21, 19 or 18, is to a good extent arbitrary, that the prime consideration seems to be the maturity or the responsibility of the person who is about to cast a vote. The question of the maturity, the ability or the understanding of a voter is of necessity a very subjective one, rather than objective. Most of us in this house at least like to think that we can remember the days of our youth and our own particular abilities. Some of us were very active in various organizations before our twenty first birthday, and I am sure that there is hardly anybody in this house who did not become most impatient with the slowness, if not the stupidity, of those who could not see things as clearly as we could. I am reminded of the story of the young fellow who, in speaking of his father said: "When I was 16, my dad didn't know a thing; by the time I was 21 I was amazed at how much the old boy had learned".
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure whether the magic age of 21 brings that realization. There are various ways in which maturity is demonstrated. There are various facets of character and intelligence which lead other people to judge one's age or maturity on different levels and for different reasons. For instance, on occasion, I have heard the hon. member for Kootenay West described by some people as the youngest member in the house. Some feel that the sense of humour he sometimes exhibits could belong to the very young because it is so bright and fresh. I have heard others say that they feel a little annoyed that this stigma can only belong to those who are too old to be here. However, I think that to consider what should be done, and at what age, would require computing machines of the type necessary to put a rocket into orbit. To try to arrive sensibly and logically at a subject which is going to be governed, as is this one, by the feeling of the majority of the people which you get on one side or the other seems to be a sort of hopeless task. The hon. member for Oxford described it in one sentence when he said that those who have finished their training are probably more apt to have the necessary maturity. I can see my brother in Edmonton, who is just starting law at the age of 40 squirm. I think he took that course because he felt no one had enough intelligence to keep up with his three sharp kids in grade ten, and wanted extra education.
I do not think that this question is just one of maturity or intelligence. I think I am

informed enough on the subject to know sufficient about young people, and I am sure that many children in their late teens are actually capable of sounder thought than some of us at a later age. I know that the question of maturity is not one that stops at 21; in most cases it goes on quite late into life. I know from my criminal law practice at home that many a man in his middle thirties, who was in trouble for the first time in his life, owed it to the fact that he suddenly started to mature and to realize, perhaps for the first time, how many years he had gone on facing life's difficulties without really realizing what they were. Then he got old, or wise enough to realize how little he had accomplished and how much more he might have done, and went to pieces.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the question of reaching the age of maturity turns on looking frankly at one's responsibilities. I suggest that in this day and age life is much more complicated than it ever has been before. It requires more years of education merely to be able to hold one's own, to have any assurance of holding a job or progressing in one's daily work. The problems we face in our day to day life are necessarily more complex because the means of mass communication are more a part of every day life. We are not confined, as we were some years ago, to merely local problems; but every day, whether in school, radio, television, or in every walk of life, the troubles from every part of the world are brought home to us. I suggest that to lower the voting age when there are so many complicating factors which make it harder for a young person to get a proper perspective in life is not being completely realistic. When I suggest that we go slow in dropping the age of 18, there are some very good, valid and substantial reasons. Of course, they do not convince me that we cannot do this; they merely convince me that I would have some hesitation in voting on the question.
I feel that there are many members in this house, perhaps more experienced in psychology and experienced in other walks of life than I, who might be able to contribute something to this discussion, but I suggest that when the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) talks of the responsibilities of democracy and of giving voting privileges to young people to add a sense of responsibility, he is only meeting half the problem. I think something is wrong in giving a person too easily the privilege of voting. There is something to be said for the right of earning the vote. Even if it is earning it merely by waiting two or three years, that in itself may be enough. May I call it six o'clock?
